title: To Jorge de Tovar
text:
This is the only man worthy of this age,

        vile tribune of the Judaic rabble,

        who does not know God, though he dares against Him,

        thieving secretary, artisan rabbi.


        Stubborn henchman, true Longinus,

        in our redemption let him try his lance,

        the one who swore lightly a thousand years ago

        because his month has come a thousand times.


        O Jew disordered by a rule!

        What wonder that they deny you what you ask,

        if you ask for the cross you are denying?


        Build houses and profit from what was stolen,

        and since you measure your faith by our life,

        if he is baptized, tell us when.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Villamediana's hostile anti-Jewish court invective as historical source language, without endorsement.

title: To a Lady Who Made Herself Available for Money
text:
The club always enters the maiden

        when the man has not failed in golds;

        swords are her discarded fare,

        because her mother wants it so.


        The malilla, though she ceases to have it,

        will not lose, so much has entered her;

        and if she wants to choose, because she has robbed,

        he is the cup and she the malilla.


        Whoever enters to play, whoever is a man,

        if he is not ready to triumph with golds,

        should never hope to win this stake.


        An extra card does not replace money

        in this hand; rather, whoever gives it

        lays his club on top of the malilla.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the bawdy satire's Spanish-card suits and malilla game term, where money and sex overlap.

title: To Josefa Vaca, Reprimanded by Her Husband
text:
"Listen, Josefa, and take care, for now you tread

        this court of the king; have prudence;

        remember that the crowd takes revenge by murmuring,

        and time always warns without speaking.


        By our holy and heavenly emblem,

        refrain from speaking with princes,

        and though one duke and another come to see you,

        let your husband be all: your honor, your mass."


        Morales said this and prayed his little prayer,

        but Josefa answers him angrily:

        "Oh, may the devil take so much bogeyman-guarding!


        Curse me if I were any more honorable!"

        But since she is simple and he is mad,

        she looked sideways, left, and nothing happened.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the comic dialogue of reputation, court gossip, and Josefa's impatient retort.

title: To a Worthy Friend Poorly Rewarded
text:
Fabio, I neither lament you as unfortunate,

        nor does the clamor of your justice distress me,

        for when malice hands out prizes,

        in the just man it is an honor not to be rewarded.


        If ignorance has granted memory,

        written in golden letters, to greed,

        what does the wise man await? Let him owe to injustice

        the pleasure of living disillusioned.


        It is inevitable that grief will defeat you

        if you pass from complaint into impatience;

        no, Fabio, your prudence is braver.


        You think heaven neglects something,

        you judge that punishment is not certain here;

        you know how little violence lasts.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the consolation that injustice can teach a wise, disillusioned prudence.

title: Josefa Vaca, Actress
editorial_note: The translation keeps Villamediana's place-name wordplay largely intact, since the satire depends on those proper names.
